overview.text: Ferromagnetism is a form of magnetism found in materials such as iron, cobalt, and nickel. Quantum-mechanical interactions make neighboring atomic magnetic moments—arising partly from electron spins—align within small regions called domains. In an unmagnetized piece, domains point in different directions, so their effects largely cancel; an applied field can shift and reorient domains, creating strong net magnetization. Ferromagnetic materials can retain magnetization after the field is removed. This history-dependent response is called hysteresis and makes magnetic recording possible. Ferromagnetism disappears above a material-specific Curie temperature, when thermal motion disrupts long-range magnetic order.

key_facts.text: Within each magnetic domain, many atomic magnetic moments align in the same direction; a domain therefore has a net magnetic moment.
A bulk ferromagnetic object can have little net magnetization when its domains point in different directions, even though each domain is magnetized.
An applied magnetic field can reorient domains and enlarge those pointing with the field, producing strong net magnetization.
Hysteresis means magnetization depends on the material’s magnetic history; some magnetization can remain after the applied field is removed.
Above a material’s Curie temperature, ferromagnetic order disappears; iron, cobalt, and nickel are examples of ferromagnetic elements.
